crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Drafting proposals from past work covers the reuse of prior aims, methods, preliminary results, budgets, and biosketches in a new grant submission. It applies to resubmissions, renewals, and new calls that extend an earlier project. The practice is not copying, it is adapting and citing material so the new proposal stands on its own. A source base can include a library of 135 research papers, prior proposals, progress reports, and reviewer comments.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on reference managers, document editors, and structured templates that keep sections aligned with a funder's instructions. Common tools include Zotero or Mendeley for citations, Word or Google Docs for drafting, and LaTeX for mathematical or technical proposals. Grant management portals such as Grants.gov and Research.gov handle submission and compliance checks. Version control and shared folders help teams track changes across coauthors and institutions.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with an inventory of past papers, proposals, and progress reports, then extracts claims, methods, and results that match the new call. Writers map each reused element to the new aims and update numbers, dates, and citations. They run a compliance check against the funder's instructions and a similarity check against the source material. The draft then goes through internal review by coauthors, department staff, and research administrators before submission.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk include copyright transfer agreements, funder open access policies, and institutional review of overlapping submissions. Provenance matters because reused text and results must be traceable to the original paper or report. Teams often keep a reuse log that records the source, license, and permission status for each borrowed passage. They also disclose prior support and check for conflicts of interest or duplicate funding.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more structured reuse, with persistent identifiers and machine readable metadata linking claims to their sources. AI assistants are being used to suggest reusable passages and to check compliance, while humans remain responsible for accuracy and attribution. Funders are moving toward open science and data sharing, which changes what can be reused and how it must be cited. The practice is likely to become more auditable, with provenance logs and version histories as standard parts of a proposal file.
